Retting.deeper: In a bast stem, fiber bundles are held to the surrounding tissues and the woody core by pectin-rich middle lamellae and hemicelluloses. Retting microbes secrete pectinases and xylanases that break down these cementing polysaccharides while, ideally, leaving the cellulose of the fibers intact. In dew retting, pulled flax lies in swaths and aerobic plant-degrading fungi colonize the stems in succession, with Cladosporium and Alternaria prominent, alongside bacterial communities that high-throughput sequencing studies now follow through the process. Water retting is anaerobic and bacterial, traditionally driven by Clostridium species that ferment pectin to organic acids. Timing is the critical control: under-retted stems resist mechanical separation, while prolonged retting allows microbial attack on the fibers themselves. Research on enzyme treatments and on inoculating dew-retting flax with Bacillus strains aims to make the process faster and more uniform.
Retting.origins: The verb ret entered English in the medieval period from Middle Dutch reeten, with relatives in Middle Low German roten and Old Norse reyta, traced to a reconstructed Proto-Germanic verb meaning to make soft or mellow. Merriam-Webster dates the first known English use to the 14th century. The word therefore names the purpose of the process, softening stems until fiber can be freed, rather than one method, and it covers both field (dew) retting and retting in ponds, rivers or tanks.

Scouring.deeper: Raw-wool scouring passes fleece through a series of warm aqueous bowls. Detergent emulsifies the water-insoluble wool grease while suint salts dissolve, and grease recovered from the liquor becomes lanolin. The effluent is among the more difficult industrial wastewaters: wool wax is held in a stable oil-in-water emulsion by nonionic detergent, and the stream is high in chemical oxygen demand, ammonia, salinity and potassium. CSIRO researchers showed that aerobic microbes can destabilize the emulsion, partly by cleaving wax esters and shortening the detergent's ethoxylate chains; in batch tests centrifuging then removed 97 percent of wool wax and 87 percent of COD. Tertiary oxidation with hydrogen peroxide and UV light brought total COD removal from raw effluent to about 97.5 percent, and a 2026 pilot biofilm reactor removed more than 91 percent of ammonia nitrogen. In cotton, scouring instead uses alkali to strip waxes and pectins before dyeing.
Scouring.origins: Cleaning fiber and cloth is ancient: Roman fullers used urine and absorbent clays, including the clay still called fuller's earth, to remove grease. Modern scouring shifted to detergents and multi-bowl machines, and the environmental burden moved to the effluent. Much of the treatment research came from CSIRO in Australia in the 2000s, where work on the Sirolan effluent process combined chemical flocculation, biological treatment and oxidation.

Scutching.deeper: Scutching exploits a mechanical contrast between the brittle, lignified woody core and the flexible fiber bundles around it. Retted straw is first broken between fluted rollers so that the core cracks into short fragments (shive), then rotating beaters strike the stems while the fiber is held, knocking shive out. The outputs are long scutched fiber, which is hackled into line, shorter scutching tow, and shive as a by-product. Results depend on retting: under-retted stems resist separation, while over-retting weakens the fiber. Plant traits matter too. In a 2018 study that scutched hemp on flax machinery, yellow-stem varieties showed higher scutching efficiency than green-stem ones, and fiber from controlled dew retting gave a higher yield of hackled fiber than un-retted fiber that was bio-degummed after scutching. Hemp stalks are roughly one fifth bast fiber and four fifths woody hurd by mass, which is why separation efficiency governs yield.
Scutching.origins: For most of its history, flax dressing (pulling, retting, breaking, scutching, hackling) was done by hand within households and local workshops. Mechanization concentrated scutching in dedicated mills, and northwestern Europe retains a long-established growing and scutching industry. The stage still defines regional identity: European origin marks for flax and linen differ in whether they cover only cultivation and scutching or also spinning, weaving and finishing.

Sliver.deeper: Most of what happens to sliver is drafting. Draft is the ratio of delivery to feed surface speed and, ignoring waste, equals input linear density divided by output linear density. At the drawframe several slivers are fed together while being drafted, a doubling that averages out thick and thin places and straightens fibers. The nip spacing is set somewhat longer than the longest fibers so no fiber is gripped by both nips at once. From there, ring spinning needs a roving stage, typically with a draft of roughly 6 to 15, whereas rotor spinning feeds drawn sliver straight to the spinning unit. On the worsted route, pinned gill boxes control long wool fibers during drafting, and the fineness of combed wool sliver is measured by airflow under IWTO-6. Evenness is reported as the coefficient of mass variation and counts of thick places, thin places and neps.
Sliver.origins: Roller drafting was the central idea of the mechanized spinning machines of eighteenth-century England, replacing the hand spinner's fingers drawing fibers from a distaff. The older verb draw survives in the names drawframe and drawing, while technicians use draft for the numerical ratio. Sliver is the continuous strand those machines were built to handle, carried between stages in cans and, for wool, formed into top.

Staple.deeper: Staple length is a distribution. For cotton, the High Volume Instrument measures bundles and reports upper half mean length, uniformity index and short fiber content, while AFIS measures single fibers and adds neps per gram and maturity. In a genome-wide study of 348 US upland cotton lines grown in 10 environments, length, strength and uniformity were positively correlated with one another and negatively with short fiber content, and all showed broad-sense heritability above 60 percent. USDA classing describes upland cotton at about 7/8 to 1 5/16 inches and American Pima at about 1 1/4 to 1 9/16 inches. Length matters because staple yarn holds together only through twist-generated friction, and drafting nips must be set longer than the longest fibers; short fibers float between nips and create unevenness. Manufactured staple is cut from filament tow and usually crimped for cohesion, which ASTM D3937 measures as crimp frequency.
Staple.origins: In the wool trade a staple is a naturally formed lock of fibers in the fleece, and classers long judged fleeces by counting crimp waves along it. In cotton the word became a measured grade: USDA classification reports staple length in fractions of an inch, so a cotton's staple is a measured value for a specific lot, not a fixed property of its name. For manufactured fibers, staple simply denotes filament deliberately cut to a finite length so it can be processed on natural-fiber spinning systems.
